newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Reformist Constantinescu takes Romania oath.
newsitem.headline: Reformist Constantinescu takes Romania oath.

text.p: Reformist Emil Constantinescu, who ousted ex-Communists in Romania's elections this month, took the oath as president on Friday, pledging to seek prosperity for the country and move it towards NATO and the European Union.

His right hand on the constitution, Constantinescu pledged during a ceremony in the opulent palace built by Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu "to devote all my strength and my abilities to the prosperity of the Romanian people".
It was Romania's first peaceful transfer of power in more than 50 years.

Constantinescu, 57, a former university rector elected seven years after the bloody revolt which ousted Ceausescu, said the transition after his win this month had been "a crucial test for democracy".

"We must revive Romania's European status. We need an economic framework for free actions which will benefit and protect everyone," he told deputies seated in a vast columned hall capped by a glass dome.
"People should not live in fear of tomorrow," he said. "We must move towards European and Atlantic institutions.
"If we succeed, the rewards will be great. If not, we will not be forgiven. There will be no excuse for failing to serve the national interest."
Constantinescu's defeat of Ion Iliescu, who had held office since 1989, was viewed by liberals as the logical outcome of the revolt they said was hijacked by Communists to keep power.

He and the centrist coalition which ousted Iliescu's leftists from government in general elections have pledged to speed up reforms to upgrade some of the lowest living standards in post-Communist eastern Europe.
Constantinescu held his first official talks with political parties after being sworn in.

The government, expected to be named imminently, will be made up of his centrist Democratic Convention, Social Democrats and leaders of the 1.6 million Hungarian minority. It is committed to imposing financial discipline and liberalising markets while increasing benefits for the needy.
Bucharest Mayor Victor Ciorbea, designated as prime minister, has promised to carry into government the sweeping anti-corruption campaign he led in the capital's city hall.

Analysts have said Romania's new leadership will boost the country's chances of being included in the first wave of NATO expansion next year, though it remains a longshot alongside favourites Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary.
Western financial institutions must also be persuaded that the government is serious about accelerating reform.
A delegation from the International Monetary Fund, which suspended credits to Romania this year over policy differences, is to hold talks with the new leaders next week.

Constantinescu said it was ironic that the orderly transfer of power was taking place in the 3,000-room stone building constructed by Ceausescu as a "People's Palace" after he issued orders to tear down a third of Bucharest's city centre.
"Modern history has brought us to a place intended for an abusive, megalomaniac and totalitarian power built to hold the people in contempt, far from the citadel of power," he said.
"Our duty is not to destroy or bury the past, but to enrich it by transforming this place into a symbol of democracy."
The palace, a maze of marble corridors and staircases lit by sumptuous chandeliers, houses the lower house of parliament. The upper house is also due to move in.
